assessment.nobel_worthiness: Legal origins and investor protection created a large empirical and conceptual research program on how legal institutions shape financial development, ownership structure and growth. The work is very widely cited and has changed both academic practice and policy debate.
assessment.attribution: The La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny collaboration is tightly integrated. Vishny's contribution is clear, especially on corporate governance, but the three-person limit forces a choice. I propose the three principal authors of the cross-country legal-origins papers.
assessment.maturity: The foundational papers date from the late 1990s. Several decades of replication, critique and extension give an unusually long evaluation period.
uncertainties: The legal-origins hypothesis has been challenged on identification, measurement and causal interpretation, and part of the literature has moved away from it.
Vishny's omission is a real attribution cost.
Reputational and ethical controversies around one candidate could weigh on committee deliberation.
Possible overlap with prior prizes in corporate finance and institutions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the study of trade shocks reshaped how economists understand labor demand, polarization, wage inequality and the distributional costs of globalization. The work is empirically credible and has had large influence on policy.
assessment.attribution: Katz is credited for the long-running work on skill demand and the race between education and technology. Autor and Hanson are credited for the task and import-competition work. Dorn is an important co-author on the China shock papers but is left out by the three-name limit.
assessment.maturity: The research spans roughly 1990s to the 2020s. The China shock and task-polarization findings have been replicated and extended for a decade or more, and the debates are now well developed.
uncertainties: Some of the task framework builds on earlier work by others outside this candidate, such as Acemoglu's, so overlap with the 2024 and 2025 prizes is a consideration.
The size and persistence of the China shock effects remain debated.
Excluding Dorn is an attribution risk.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection moved international trade from sector-level to firm-level analysis. It identified new gains from trade through reallocation and set the basis for modern quantitative trade work. The conceptual contribution is clear and well tested.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple and related work extend it, and Redding contributes on quantitative spatial and trade extensions. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not on this ballot but worked on closely related ideas, so credit is somewhat diffuse.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of empirical validation, extension and policy use. The prize is natural after Krugman's 2008 prize.
uncertainties: Priority questions with related firm-level trade work not credited on this ballot.
Some gains-from-trade results depend on functional form, as the quantitative trade debate shows.
Helpman's contributions are also split across other candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Resource misallocation across firms and sectors offers a quantitative account of cross-country TFP and income differences. It changed development and growth accounting by giving a measurable, microdata-based mechanism, and it spawned a large literature.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the central paper and Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) is the parallel source. Rogerson is not credited on this ballot, which is an attribution gap. Restuccia's agricultural productivity and misallocation work complements the other two.
assessment.maturity: More than fifteen years of work. The misallocation literature has been heavily scrutinized, including for measurement error, and has survived in a refined form.
uncertainties: Measurement sensitivity: markup and wedge estimates are affected by data error and model assumptions.
Restuccia and Rogerson's priority is not reflected in the credited names.
Disclosed conflict: this member is a long-running co-author of Klenow. It is disclosed, not adjudicated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities, together with the Taylor rule, is the standard workhorse of monetary policy analysis in central banks. The influence on practice and theory is very large.
assessment.attribution: Highly diffuse across at least eight credited names, including Calvo, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets. Any three-person selection omits major contributors. Woodford (synthesis), Gali (NK model and empirical evidence) and Taylor (rules) represent different strands.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with more than twenty-five years of use in policy. Foundational contributions are old and the framework is deeply established.
uncertainties: Substantial attribution difficulty and risk of overlap with Rational expectations, Lucas and Bernanke-related prizes.
Post-2008 and post-2021 inflation episodes have prompted criticism of the framework's adequacy.
Gertler and Calvo are strong alternatives.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Tying optimal tax theory to empirical elasticities, notably the elasticity of taxable income and sufficient-statistics methods, gave public finance a practical bridge between theory and measurement. The work has shaped academic and policy discussion of top rates and tax design.
assessment.attribution: Slemrod has the earlier and foundational work on behavioral responses to taxation. Saez is the central figure on optimal tax and top incomes, while Chetty contributes the sufficient-statistics approach. Stantcheva is much more recent. Saez and Chetty also appear on other ballots, so credit is split across several strands.
assessment.maturity: Core work is from the 1990s to the 2010s and well tested. Stantcheva's contributions are comparatively early for recognition.
uncertainties: Estimates of the elasticity of taxable income remain contested, particularly at the top.
Overlap with the inequality and mobility candidates raises the risk of splitting credit.
The proposed trio blends senior foundational and mid-career work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) formalized how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. The financial-accelerator and credit-cycle line became central to macro-finance and to understanding crises, and it informs how policy models treat financial frictions.
assessment.attribution: The collateral-constraint mechanism is cleanly attributable to Kiyotaki and Moore. Gertler and Gilchrist developed the financial-accelerator and empirical strands, and Bernanke already received the 2022 prize for related work. I propose the two with the clearest theoretical priority.
assessment.maturity: The paper is nearly thirty years old and has been extended widely and tested in macro and corporate finance models. It is timely in light of recent crises.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banking and financial crises may reduce its relative standing.
Excluding Gertler and Gilchrist is an attribution cost.
The empirical identification of collateral effects is still under discussion.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Household debt and credit supply shocks are shown to drive the real economy, using granular microdata on mortgage credit, housing and consumption. The work changed the analysis of the Great Recession and the macroeconomics of leverage.
assessment.attribution: Mian and Sufi are clearly the core pair and their work is closely joint. Campbell is a major finance scholar but his credited link to this theme is less central, so I propose only the two.
assessment.maturity: The central papers date from about 2009 to 2015 and have been replicated and debated for over a decade. This is relatively young by prize standards but sufficient for recognition.
uncertainties: Debates continue about the causal role of credit supply versus other factors in the housing boom and bust.
Possible overlap with the 2022 prize and with the macro-finance literature more generally.
Time since publication is shorter than for other candidates, so a later year may be more appropriate.
